decision.location: Section 2.3 Individual differences (line 109, chunk 21); Section 4 Results (line 153)
decision.quote: Crutchfield [ 8 ] studied the effect of intellectual competence on conformity. He found that higher competence was associated with lower levels of conformity. However, intelligence was measured by the subjective ratings of the experimental staff. Iscoe, Williams, and Harvey [ 10 ] exposed high school students (7 to 15 years) to group pressure in an acoustic task (counting metronome ticks), and approximated intelligence by subjects’ school records. They found no correlation of school records with conformity. Uchida et al. [ 31 ] studied 12 to 14 year-old high school students and assessed scholastic achievements by their school performance. They report that high achievers conformed less to the majority than low achievers. Hence, results of the effect of intelligence on conformity are inconclusive so far and the existing studies use indirect measures (school grades) but do not measure intelligence directly.
decision.reason: The current paper explicitly treats Uchida et al. scholastic achievement as an indirect intelligence measure motivating H5, and tests a negative fluid-intelligence/conformity association. The complete original does report an overall high-/low-achievement conformity difference, as well as conditional minority/majority status effects; it is therefore too strong to exclude it merely because no IQ test or peer-status manipulation is repeated. Yet the original operationalises attained school achievement and hypothesised status/confidence, while the current regression operationalises adult matrix intelligence without achievement or group status. The current source supplies no original-specific results comparison resolving whether this is an empirical conceptual retest of that attainment finding or a new latent-cognitive claim prompted by the literature. This is a genuine construct/finding correspondence ambiguity in two available complete reports, not an original access limit and not a methods-difference exclusion. Original-only group-composition findings are not transferred.

corrected_value.title: The effects of self-consciousness and self-esteem on conformity to a majority

decision.location: Section 2.3 Individual differences (line 110, chunk 22); Section 4 Results (lines 153, 164)
decision.quote: The effect of self-esteem (or self-assertiveness, self-consciousness) on conformity was only investigated in a few studies so far. Kurosawa [ 11 ] found no effect on conformity when the decision of the minority subject was preceded by two confederates. In groups of four, confederates’ self-esteem had a negative effect on conformity. Similarly, Tainaka et al. [ 32 ] found in a sample of Japanese female students that those with low self-esteem conformed more often in a co-witness task.
decision.reason: The journal-hosted primary English abstract positively reports that responding students with higher self-esteem conformed less under four preceding unanimous wrong answers. Current H6 explicitly predicts the same participant-self-esteem association after reviewing Kurosawa, and Methods put the naive respondent in seat5, with four confederates answering before that participant. The current Rosenberg regression therefore empirically retests the original high-pressure component; it need not also vary pressure or reproduce the other public-self-consciousness interactions to qualify. The current literature sentence mistakenly calls this confederates’ self-esteem; that wording remains unchanged, but does not erase the independently verified original actor or the actual current hypothesis, measurement and response-position correspondence. The Japanese body remains unavailable after recorded attempts; exact original scale/statistics are not claimed. Tainaka2014 instead supplies a co-witness memory component, cites no Kurosawa in its complete text, and is not positively documented as an intervening retest of this high-pressure line-judgment finding. No report or participant independence is inferred from dates. Shipped row6 Asch1956 does not represent Kurosawa. No outcome requested.

decision.reason: The complete published Hackl2009 body now removes the former local-text gap. Its own SPC experiments empirically show quantifier-dependent intermediate processing profiles for truth-conditionally equivalent most/more-than-half judgments on the same arrays, despite nonsignificant overall accuracy/RT. The current within-subject Most1/Most2 comparison on identical two-color displays also holds truth conditions constant and tests whether lexical quantifier semantics forces different verification profiles; the conclusion expressly confirms and extends Hackl. It is a conceptual retest of this lexical computational nonequivalence component, not a claimed reproduction of the original particular lead-counting versus half-criterion algorithm or incremental timing statistic. Changed quantifiers, flash presentation and performance measure do not alone exclude that test. Lidz2011 explicitly discusses Hackl but its own experiment varies color diversity for most alone: it is the closest subtraction/color-invariance comparison, already row2248, rather than an intervening experiment comparing two lexical quantifiers. Thus Hackl adds an independently attributed original-specific comparison absent from the represented Lidz row. Current true/false directional reversal, nonsignificant language-specific RTs and formula/prose inconsistency remain; no outcome, participant independence, or identical algorithm is inferred.
